summary.text: The law of conservation of mass says that in a system closed to matter moving in or out, the total mass stays constant over time.
In a chemical reaction, the mass of the starting materials equals the mass of the products, since mass may be rearranged or changed in form but not created or destroyed.
Accepting it helped chemistry progress from alchemy, though the law holds only in the classical limit.

facts.label: Closed systems
facts.value: No matter moves in or out, so mass stays constant

facts.label: Early demonstrators
facts.value: Jean Rey in 1630, confirmed by Lavoisier in the late 1700s

facts.label: Theory it disproved
facts.value: Phlogiston, which said mass could be gained or lost in burning

facts.label: Stas's precision
facts.value: Loss or gain in certain reactions was at most 2 to 4 parts in 100,000

facts.label: Why it stayed hidden
facts.value: The atmosphere's buoyancy affects the weight of gases

items.prompt: An iron nail rusts inside a sealed glass tube. How does the weight of the tube and its contents compare before and after?

options.label: Heavier, since rust is bulkier than iron
Lighter, since the nail wears away
Heavier at first, then lighter again
The same, since nothing enters or leaves

items.explain: Rusting in a sealed glass tube did not change the weight of the container and its contents, because the system is closed to matter moving in or out.

items.prompt: For thousands of years people saw that a burned log weighs less than the log did. Why did that mislead them about mass?

options.label: Air's buoyancy distorted the weight of gases
Wood truly loses mass whenever it burns
Scales could not weigh any solid at all
Heat carries mass away as invisible light

items.explain: The conservation of mass was obscure because of the buoyancy effect of the atmosphere on the weight of gases, so burned wood seemed to lose mass.

items.prompt: A gas burner burns methane with oxygen. The mixture starts with 1 carbon atom, 4 hydrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms and ends with 1 carbon dioxide molecule plus water. How many water molecules must form?

options.label: Four
Three
Two
One

items.explain: Since the same atoms must be present at the end, the water molecules produced must be exactly two per molecule of carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: To show by weighing that mass stays constant during a reaction, what must you do with the reacting material?

options.label: Leave it open so gases can drift in and out
Keep it closed off so no matter enters or leaves
Heat it long enough to finish the reaction
Weigh only the starting materials twice

items.explain: The law applies to a system closed to incoming and outgoing transfers of matter; mass is not generally conserved in open systems.

items.prompt: In the 1700s a popular theory held that burning and heating could add or remove mass. How did the careful tests of mass conservation affect it?

options.label: They backed it up, showing mass is gained in heating
They narrowed it to apply only to metals
They left it untouched, as it covered burning only
They disproved it, showing mass is not gained or lost

items.explain: The demonstrations of the principle disproved the phlogiston theory, which said mass could be gained or lost in combustion and heat processes.

items.prompt: A PET scan relies on an electron and a positron, nearly at rest, annihilating into two photons. What does that say about the law of conservation of mass?

options.label: It holds only in the classical limit, so mass is not always conserved
It holds everywhere, so the photons must be hiding the mass
It applies only to systems that contain photons
It fails only in open systems, and this one must have been open

items.explain: In general mass is not conserved; the law holds only in the classical limit, and electron-positron annihilation is an example.
